constraints: The workload is containerized.
Kubernetes compatibility is not a requirement.
The team wants AWS-native orchestration with less control-plane administration.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: ECS reduces Kubernetes-specific overhead, while EKS can be justified by Kubernetes ecosystem, portability, or organizational standardization.
details.errorCorrection: EKS is not automatically simpler, EC2 Auto Scaling does not orchestrate service placement alone, and S3 stores images or definitions but does not schedule workloads.
details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS manages container tasks and services using AWS constructs; EKS provides a managed Kubernetes control plane but still requires Kubernetes-oriented platform design and operations.
details.scenarioApplication: The team runs ECS services, selects an appropriate capacity provider, and uses AWS IAM, networking, deployment, and observability integrations.

messages.text: EKS still has Kubernetes platform and workload-operating considerations; it is not universally simpler.
EC2 Auto Scaling changes instance capacity but does not replace a container orchestrator's scheduling and service model.
S3 is storage and does not run or schedule containers.

feedback.reason: ECS is an AWS-native container orchestrator and can be a better fit when Kubernetes APIs or portability are not required and operational simplicity matters.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon ECS because it provides AWS-native container orchestration without requiring the team to adopt a Kubernetes control-plane operating model.
Choose EKS automatically because Kubernetes is always less operational work than an AWS-native orchestrator.
Choose EC2 Auto Scaling alone because it schedules containers and performs service discovery without an orchestrator.
Choose S3 because container images and task definitions are both object-storage concerns.

prompt: A team needs to run containers on AWS, has no requirement for Kubernetes APIs, and wants the smallest platform operations surface. Which service should be evaluated first?

constraints: The component is a long-running service.
Desired count and health matter.
Tasks should be replaced automatically.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The service model handles replacement but does not make the application stateful or idempotent; data must be owned by appropriate durable services.
details.errorCorrection: A standalone task does not maintain availability, S3 is not scheduling state, and EBS snapshots do not orchestrate containers.
details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS task definitions describe containers; an ECS service schedules tasks, maintains desired count, integrates with load balancing, and handles deployments and health checks.
details.scenarioApplication: The team defines the task resources and ports, configures the service desired count and deployment limits, and routes traffic only to healthy tasks.

messages.text: A standalone task leaves replacement and desired capacity to manual operations.
ECS scheduling state is not stored or controlled by an arbitrary S3 object.
Snapshots store block data and do not define or restart an ECS service.

feedback.reason: An ECS service maintains desired running tasks and coordinates deployment and replacement behavior for a long-running component.

options.text: Define an ECS service using a task definition, desired count, deployment configuration, networking, and health checks so the scheduler maintains the service.
Run one standalone ECS task and manually start a replacement after every failure.
Store the desired count in an S3 object because ECS reads scheduling state from object storage.
Use an EBS snapshot as the service definition because storage snapshots restart containers automatically.

prompt: A web component should maintain a desired number of healthy container instances and replace tasks that stop unexpectedly. Which ECS construct should represent it?

constraints: AWS manages the EKS control plane service.
Worker capacity and workloads still belong to the customer design.
The team must operate applications reliably.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: EKS reduces control-plane administration but retains Kubernetes expertise and platform responsibility; that cost must be part of the service choice.
details.errorCorrection: Managed control plane does not mean managed application stack, the control plane does not run pods as compute, and public subnets are not required for workloads.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The managed control plane includes Kubernetes management components, while nodes or serverless pod capacity, cluster networking, IAM, add-ons, and application resources remain part of the solution.
details.scenarioApplication: The team selects managed node groups or another capacity model, installs required add-ons, applies least-privilege pod access, and tests upgrades and failure recovery.

messages.text: AWS does not automatically own every worker, add-on, workload, or data-store concern in an EKS design.
The control plane schedules and manages pods but is not the application compute capacity.
Pods can use private networking; public addressing is not a requirement for control-plane management.

feedback.reason: EKS manages the Kubernetes control plane, but the customer still designs and operates worker capacity, workloads, integrations, and application data.

options.text: Treat EKS as a managed Kubernetes control plane while still planning node or serverless compute, networking, IAM, add-ons, workload health, upgrades, and observability.
Assume AWS provisions and patches every worker, application container, add-on, and data store automatically with no customer choices.
Use the EKS control plane as the workload compute layer because Kubernetes API capacity runs application pods by itself.
Place all pods in a public subnet because EKS control-plane management requires public application addresses.

prompt: A team adopts Amazon EKS and assumes that a managed control plane removes all cluster operations. Which statement should correct the design?

constraints: Kubernetes APIs and tooling are established requirements.
Portability is valuable.
The team accepts Kubernetes platform operations.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: EKS preserves ecosystem alignment but carries Kubernetes complexity and portability is never absolute when cloud-specific integrations are used.
details.errorCorrection: ECS is not a Kubernetes cluster, Lambda does not execute Helm manifests, and S3 stores artifacts rather than scheduling them.
details.mechanismOrProperty: EKS provides a managed Kubernetes control plane, allowing the organization to use Kubernetes resource models and ecosystem integrations while managing workload capacity and platform choices.
details.scenarioApplication: The team validates add-on, networking, identity, storage, and upgrade compatibility rather than assuming every chart is portable without changes.

messages.text: ECS uses its own task and service model and does not run Kubernetes manifests directly.
Lambda runtimes do not execute Helm charts as an orchestration system.
Object storage can hold manifests but cannot provide cluster scheduling or service health.

feedback.reason: EKS is the natural candidate when Kubernetes APIs, tooling, and portability are explicit constraints.

options.text: Evaluate EKS because it provides managed Kubernetes control-plane infrastructure while preserving the Kubernetes API and ecosystem the organization already operates.
Choose ECS because it can run every Kubernetes manifest without conversion or Kubernetes-specific tooling.
Choose Lambda because Helm charts are directly executed by Lambda runtimes.
Choose S3 because portable manifests should not be scheduled by a cluster.

prompt: A company has a large Kubernetes platform team, standardized Helm charts, and a requirement to keep deployment manifests portable across multiple Kubernetes environments. Which choice is most aligned?

constraints: Traffic goes through a load balancer.
The service must maintain availability during deployment.
Health checks must influence replacement.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A conservative deployment consumes extra capacity during rollout; the team must size capacity and choose a strategy consistent with availability objectives.
details.errorCorrection: Simultaneous replacement creates an outage, in-place image mutation removes reproducibility, and storage snapshots do not perform service rollout.
details.mechanismOrProperty: An ECS service uses task definitions, deployment configuration, and health checks to start, validate, and stop task instances; load balancer health can prevent traffic from reaching unhealthy tasks.
details.scenarioApplication: The team sets safe healthy-capacity bounds, deploys a revision, observes task and target health, and rolls back or stops the rollout on failure.

messages.text: Replacing all tasks simultaneously can remove serving capacity and does not provide a controlled rollout.
Immutable task definitions preserve deployment identity and rollback; mutating images in place is not a reliable rollout model.
EBS snapshots store data and do not evaluate container health or orchestrate deployments.

feedback.reason: ECS deployment configuration and health checks control how task revisions replace one another while preserving service availability.

options.text: Configure the ECS service deployment strategy, minimum and maximum healthy percentages, load-balancer health checks, and rollback or failure handling for the new task revision.
Replace every task simultaneously and wait for clients to discover the new container IPs.
Update the container image in place without a new task definition revision so ECS cannot distinguish old and new tasks.
Use an EBS snapshot to perform the application deployment because task health is a storage property.

prompt: An ECS service must deploy a new task definition revision while keeping enough healthy capacity to serve traffic and stopping unhealthy new tasks automatically. Which design should be configured?

constraints: Control plane and data plane components have compatibility boundaries.
The cluster uses managed add-ons.
Production upgrades require a rollback or recovery plan.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Staged upgrades and parallel capacity consume resources but reduce production blast radius and make rollback or recovery more practical.
details.errorCorrection: Automatic compatibility cannot be assumed, destructive recreation loses state and evidence, and CPU does not fix API or add-on incompatibility.
details.mechanismOrProperty: EKS cluster components have version and integration dependencies; upgrade planning must cover the control plane, compute, networking, storage, identity, add-ons, and application behavior.
details.scenarioApplication: The team tests an upgrade path, updates managed node groups and add-ons in supported order, drains safely, and monitors workload health during staged rollout.

messages.text: Control-plane upgrade does not guarantee every node, add-on, or workload is compatible without validation.
Recreation without state and compatibility planning creates unnecessary outage and data risk.
Resource size cannot resolve version or API incompatibility.

feedback.reason: Managed control-plane updates do not remove compatibility and lifecycle responsibility for nodes, add-ons, and workloads.

options.text: Maintain an upgrade matrix and test control plane, node, add-on, admission, storage, and workload compatibility in a nonproduction environment before staged production rollout.
Upgrade only the control plane because Kubernetes automatically makes every node and add-on compatible immediately.
Delete and recreate the cluster for every patch without preserving workload state or validating the replacement.
Increase pod CPU so version compatibility errors become less likely.

prompt: An EKS team upgrades the Kubernetes control plane but forgets to validate node versions, networking add-ons, and workload compatibility. Which operating practice is missing?

constraints: Placement affects availability and data access.
Replicas should be distributed.
The scheduler must enforce the requirement.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Strict constraints may reduce schedulable capacity, so spare headroom and an explicit unavailable state are safer than silently violating placement.
details.errorCorrection: A load balancer cannot repair unsatisfied placement, image size is unrelated, and one Availability Zone creates a shared failure domain.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Schedulers use resource requests, constraints, placement strategies, or affinity rules to select eligible capacity; workload availability depends on the capacity and storage model supporting those rules.
details.scenarioApplication: The team spreads replicas across failure domains, verifies volume compatibility, and tests behavior when one capacity segment is unavailable.

messages.text: Traffic routing cannot compensate for replicas placed in an invalid failure or storage domain.
Image size does not determine scheduler placement.
Single-AZ placement preserves a common failure domain rather than distributing risk.

feedback.reason: Placement and resource constraints belong in the orchestrator and must be tested against capacity and failure-domain requirements.

options.text: Declare resource, affinity, and anti-affinity or placement constraints in the orchestrator and validate that the selected capacity model can satisfy them during scale and failure.
Let the scheduler place replicas arbitrarily and rely on the load balancer to move a replica after a failure.
Use a larger container image because image size determines failure-domain placement.
Put all replicas in one Availability Zone so their shared volume is always local.

prompt: A workload requires access to a specific data volume and must not place two replicas on the same failure domain. Which orchestration design should be evaluated?

constraints: The service must remain available.
New tasks need health validation.
Old tasks can be stopped only after safe replacement.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keeping extra capacity during rollout costs more but preserves availability and makes failure recovery safer.
details.errorCorrection: Stopping all old tasks creates an outage, mutating filesystems is not an immutable rollout, and zone size does not define deployment capacity.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The orchestrator starts new revisions subject to capacity limits, validates task or pod health, and removes old revisions according to deployment policy.
details.scenarioApplication: The team maintains four healthy replicas, tests the new image, and halts or rolls back if readiness or target health deteriorates.

messages.text: Stopping all old tasks removes serving capacity before the new revision is proven.
In-place mutation is not reproducible and does not create a controlled deployment revision.
Availability Zone capacity does not replace deployment health and capacity settings.

feedback.reason: Rolling deployment settings control replacement capacity and allow health checks to gate traffic and progression.

options.text: Use a rolling deployment with minimum and maximum healthy capacity settings, health checks, and a rollback or pause condition when the new tasks fail validation.
Stop all old tasks first and start new ones after the image has been copied to the registry.
Change the running container filesystem in place and assume the scheduler can observe the mutation as a new revision.
Use a larger Availability Zone because rollout safety is determined by zone size rather than healthy capacity.

prompt: A service has five replicas and must gradually replace an old image while preserving at least four healthy replicas. Which rollout concept is relevant?

constraints: Two revisions may run simultaneously.
Traffic shifting must be controlled.
Rollback should not require rebuilding the old image.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Running both revisions costs extra capacity and requires data-schema compatibility during coexistence.
details.errorCorrection: Immediate replacement loses rapid rollback, permanent unmeasured split makes attribution difficult, and route tables do not validate application health.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Two deployment environments or target groups allow independent health validation and controlled listener or routing changes; the prior environment remains available during the cutover window.
details.scenarioApplication: The team tests green, shifts a measured percentage or all traffic, monitors application and target health, and reverses the listener when error rate rises.

messages.text: Rebuilding the old version after failure slows rollback and may not reproduce the exact serving artifact.
Unmeasured permanent split obscures behavior and is not a controlled cutover.
Network route changes do not prove that the application revision is healthy.

feedback.reason: Blue-green deployment keeps old and new capacity distinct so traffic can shift after validation and roll back quickly.

options.text: Use a blue-green deployment with separate target groups or services, validate the green revision, shift traffic deliberately, and retain the blue revision until rollback risk is acceptable.
Replace the old revision immediately and reconstruct it from source only if the new revision fails.
Send production traffic to both revisions permanently without measuring which version served a response.
Use a route table change as the only deployment health check.

prompt: A team needs to validate a new container revision with production-like traffic before shifting all users, while keeping the old revision available for rapid rollback. Which pattern fits?

constraints: Task addresses change during scaling.
Callers remain private to the VPC.
Unhealthy tasks must be excluded.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: DNS caching and health-check timing affect failover, so clients still need bounded timeouts and retry behavior.
details.errorCorrection: Manual IP propagation creates deployment coupling, public IPs add unnecessary exposure, and EBS does not update discovery records.
details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS service discovery registers task endpoints and internal load balancers route to healthy targets; callers resolve a service name or use the load balancer address.
details.scenarioApplication: The service registers tasks automatically, health checks remove failing targets, and consumers use a private DNS name or internal listener.

messages.text: Restarting all callers on every task change defeats service autonomy and is operationally fragile.
Public addressing is unnecessary for private service communication and broadens exposure.
Block storage does not provide service registration or health-aware routing.

feedback.reason: Stable internal discovery or load-balancing endpoints decouple callers from ephemeral task placement.

options.text: Use an internal load balancer or ECS service discovery name with health-aware registration, so callers use a stable service endpoint rather than task IPs.
Publish every new task IP to all callers and restart them after every scale event.
Assign public IPs to tasks so callers can resolve them through the internet.
Use an EBS volume to hold the current task IP list because storage automatically updates service endpoints.

prompt: An ECS service scales from two to twenty tasks, and callers currently store task IP addresses in environment variables. What should replace that coupling?

constraints: Task permissions differ by service.
The host runs multiple workloads.
Credentials must not be embedded in the image.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Task-role design still requires careful resource policies, encryption permissions, and protection against container credential misuse.
details.errorCorrection: A broad instance role expands every task's permissions, embedded keys are long-lived secrets, and security groups do not authorize S3 API actions.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A task role supplies temporary AWS credentials to containers in that task; the role policy can be scoped to the required bucket and prefix.
details.scenarioApplication: The team grants only s3:GetObject on the needed resource, validates the task identity, and keeps the host role separate for infrastructure operations.

messages.text: A broad host role violates workload isolation and least privilege.
Embedded long-lived credentials are difficult to rotate and can leak through image or runtime access.
Security groups control network paths, not IAM authorization to S3 objects.

feedback.reason: ECS task roles isolate permissions to the workload and avoid sharing broad host credentials or static keys.

options.text: Assign a task role with only the required S3 permissions and let the task obtain temporary credentials through the ECS task role mechanism.
Attach AdministratorAccess to the EC2 instance role so every task can use the same broad permissions.
Bake a long-lived access key into the image so the task does not need an IAM role.
Use a security group to grant the task permission to read the S3 prefix.

prompt: An ECS task needs to read one S3 prefix, while the EC2 container instances run unrelated services. Which identity design is least privileged?

constraints: The password is sensitive.
Rotation must not require image rebuild.
The task should receive only its needed secret.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Runtime retrieval adds dependency and startup failure modes, so availability, caching, and rotation cutover must be tested.
details.errorCorrection: Private image storage does not make embedded secrets safe, public environment variables expose them, and route metadata is not a secret store.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Secrets Manager or Parameter Store can hold sensitive values, while IAM controls which task can read them; rotation and application refresh behavior must be designed together.
details.scenarioApplication: The task role reads one secret ARN, the service handles refresh or replacement after rotation, and logs never print the password.

messages.text: Anyone or any process with image access may retrieve an embedded credential, and rotation requires rebuilding.
Public environment variables are not an appropriate protection for a database password.
Route tables do not store secrets or provide a secure access policy.

feedback.reason: A managed secret store separates sensitive configuration from the image and supports controlled access and rotation.

options.text: Store the secret in Secrets Manager or an appropriate secure parameter store, grant the task least-privilege read access, and inject or fetch it through a controlled runtime mechanism.
Commit the password to the container image because private ECR access makes image contents secret.
Put the password in a public environment variable so all tasks receive the same rotated value.
Store the password in the route table because the task can read route metadata without credentials.

prompt: A containerized service needs a database password that rotates without rebuilding the image. Which configuration is appropriate?

constraints: The teams have distinct failure and access boundaries.
Some capacity sharing is desirable.
A cluster outage can affect all workloads in it.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More clusters increase platform cost and upgrade work; fewer clusters increase shared blast radius and governance complexity.
details.errorCorrection: One cluster is not automatically safer, one cluster per service over-fragments operations, and subnet count does not determine cluster ownership.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A cluster is an operational and failure domain. Namespaces, accounts, node groups, task roles, and network controls can isolate within a cluster, but they do not remove every shared control-plane or upgrade risk.
details.scenarioApplication: The teams score isolation and utilization needs, define least-privilege access, and use separate clusters where a shared failure or upgrade window is unacceptable.

messages.text: A shared cluster can create common failure and upgrade domains, so fewer is not automatically safer.
A cluster per service often adds unnecessary platform overhead when stronger in-cluster boundaries are sufficient.
Subnets and clusters have different architectural roles and are not one-to-one by rule.

feedback.reason: Cluster boundaries trade operational efficiency against blast-radius, security, upgrade, quota, and ownership isolation.

options.text: Choose the cluster boundary from isolation, upgrade, security, quota, operational ownership, and utilization requirements; share only what does not violate those boundaries.
Always use one cluster because fewer clusters automatically provide stronger isolation and simpler incident response.
Always use one cluster per service because any shared control plane is unsafe.
Choose the number of clusters from subnet count alone because each subnet should contain exactly one cluster.

prompt: Two teams have incompatible upgrade schedules and different production blast-radius requirements, but they want to share some platform tooling. What should influence whether they use one or multiple clusters?

constraints: The database requires durable state.
The team wants managed operations.
Container replacement must not lose committed data.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Running a database in containers may be valid for specialized control or portability, but the complete stateful operating model must be deliberate and evidenced.
details.errorCorrection: Ephemeral storage loses state, image size does not preserve database pages, and public placement is unrelated to durability.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A replaceable task filesystem is not durable database storage. Durable volumes, backup, replication, failover, patching, and restore testing are separate responsibilities from container scheduling.
details.scenarioApplication: The team uses RDS or another purpose-built managed database when it matches the engine and operations needs, and keeps containers focused on stateless or explicitly managed application work.

messages.text: Ephemeral container storage is not a durable database volume.
An image contains application artifacts and does not preserve runtime database state.
Public network placement does not provide database durability or failover.

feedback.reason: Containers can run stateful workloads, but orchestration does not automatically solve durable storage and database operations; a managed database may better fit the requirement.

options.text: Evaluate a managed database service first; use containers for the application tier unless the team can explicitly own stateful storage, backup, failover, and operational recovery requirements.
Run the database on ephemeral container storage because orchestration automatically makes all container files durable.
Use a larger container image so committed database pages survive task replacement.
Put the database in a public subnet so replacement tasks can reconstruct state from the internet.

prompt: A team wants to run a transactional database inside replaceable containers but has not designed durable storage, backup, failover, or recovery. What recommendation is strongest?

constraints: The workload has measurable memory needs.
The scheduler uses resource declarations.
Noisy-neighbor behavior must be limited.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Limits that are too low cause termination or throttling; limits too high reduce packing efficiency and can make scale-out appear unavailable.
details.errorCorrection: Unbounded consumption worsens noisy-neighbor risk, image tags do not express resource needs, and subnet placement does not provide memory capacity.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Container schedulers use declared CPU and memory requirements to place tasks or pods and enforce or report limits according to the platform mode.
details.scenarioApplication: The team measures peak memory, sets an appropriate reservation and limit, scales or right-sizes capacity, and alarms on throttling or out-of-memory termination.

messages.text: Removing limits allows one task to consume shared capacity and increases failure blast radius.
Image identity and resource requirements are separate task-definition properties.
Network placement does not determine host memory or scheduler capacity.

feedback.reason: Resource requests and limits inform scheduling and constrain noisy workloads; they must be based on measured behavior.

options.text: Set realistic CPU and memory requests or reservations and limits for the container, then validate placement, utilization, and behavior under load.
Remove all resource limits so the task can consume the entire host whenever it needs capacity.
Increase the image tag version because scheduling uses image version as the capacity signal.
Move the task to a public subnet because private placement causes memory starvation.

prompt: A container requests far less memory than it can consume, so one noisy task starves neighbors and is repeatedly killed. Which declaration should be corrected?

constraints: Process liveness is not sufficient.
Traffic should reach only ready instances.
A dependency failure should not cause endless replacement.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Deep dependency checks can create cascading replacements; health endpoints should expose the service's own ability to serve rather than every downstream detail.
details.errorCorrection: A PID does not prove request readiness, removing checks sends traffic to failing tasks, and snapshots are not service health signals.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Container and load-balancer health checks can determine whether a task receives traffic and whether the scheduler replaces it. Checks should be fast, meaningful, and aligned with startup and dependency semantics.
details.scenarioApplication: The team checks a lightweight readiness path, uses a separate liveness signal where supported, and sets thresholds that allow normal dependency recovery.

messages.text: A process can be alive while the application endpoint is unable to serve valid requests.
Without health checks, traffic and scheduler decisions cannot exclude failing tasks.
Storage snapshots do not test application request readiness.

feedback.reason: Health checks must represent the service's traffic readiness and recovery behavior, not merely process existence.

options.text: Define health checks that distinguish process liveness from readiness for traffic, use sensible failure thresholds, and avoid treating a transient dependency as an unrecoverable startup loop.
Check only whether the process has a PID because an alive process is always ready to serve.
Remove health checks so the load balancer sends traffic to every running task.
Use an EBS snapshot as the health signal because a volume snapshot proves the application can serve requests.

prompt: A container process is running but cannot reach its database and returns errors to users. The orchestrator considers it healthy because the process exists. What should be added?

constraints: The service is distributed across tasks or pods.
Logs, metrics, and deployment identity are required.
Operators need to correlate failures with a revision.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Retention and cardinality cost must be managed, but removing deployment and failure evidence makes diagnosis slower and less reliable.
details.errorCorrection: Host CPU alone misses many failure modes, deleting history removes deployment evidence, and a registry describes artifacts rather than runtime behavior.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Centralized logs and metrics expose application errors, task health, resource pressure, and rollout behavior; revision and correlation identifiers connect symptoms to a change and request.
details.scenarioApplication: The team sends stdout or structured logs to a supported sink, monitors target health and resource metrics, and retains enough history for rollout comparison.

messages.text: Host CPU cannot distinguish application errors, failed health checks, image faults, or downstream latency by itself.
Old revisions are essential evidence when a deployment introduces a failure.
An image registry has artifact metadata and does not observe live requests or container health.

feedback.reason: Container reliability requires service, workload, deployment, and platform signals that can be correlated across replacements.

options.text: Collect structured application and platform logs, task or pod and target health metrics, deployment revision identifiers, and correlation data in a centralized operational view.
Collect only host CPU because application failures always raise host CPU first.
Delete old task logs after each deployment because only the current revision can fail.
Use the container image registry as the sole source of runtime health and request metrics.

prompt: A container service scales out, but the team cannot distinguish application errors from image startup failures or host capacity pressure. Which observability design is needed?

constraints: Workload volume is modest.
The team is small.
Both compute and platform operations have value.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A more capable platform can be worthwhile for standardization or portability, but capability without a requirement can be unnecessary complexity.
details.errorCorrection: Compute price omits platform cost, EKS does not remove all worker and add-on work, and image storage is only a small part of operating cost.
details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS and EKS differ in control-plane model, worker management, add-ons, networking, observability, support, and required expertise; total cost follows the complete operating model.
details.scenarioApplication: The team estimates workload utilization and labor, validates required integrations, and selects the platform with the smallest adequate operational boundary.

messages.text: Raw vCPU price omits control-plane, idle capacity, network, tooling, and labor cost.
EKS manages a control plane but does not eliminate every worker, add-on, or platform operating cost.
Image storage cost does not represent the orchestration operating model.

feedback.reason: Container platform selection includes operational complexity and idle or shared capacity, not only raw task pricing.

options.text: Compare total cost of compute, cluster or control-plane resources, networking, logging, support, upgrades, security, and platform labor, then prefer the simpler model that satisfies the actual requirements.
Compare only per-vCPU compute price because platform operations and idle capacity have no architectural cost.
Choose EKS because Kubernetes automatically eliminates all worker and add-on operating cost.
Choose whichever service has the lower image storage price because orchestration dominates no other cost.

prompt: A small team is comparing ECS on Fargate with EKS on managed nodes for a few modest services. The workloads do not need Kubernetes APIs. Which cost boundary matters most?
